\chapter{Synthesis --- You, and Somebody Else}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-yo-go}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the same thing about myself and about someone else, and know which of the two is irregular.}

The oddity lives only in the yo slot - the form a beginner says most.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — you, and somebody else}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-sintesis-yo-go}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. Say three of the six \emph{-go} forms, whichever come first.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the odd slot is the one about you}]
Here is the practical shape of what you have, and it is worth noticing before you use it.

These six verbs are irregular \textbf{only when you talk about yourself.} Every one of them behaves normally the moment the sentence is about anybody else:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{salgo} — but \emph{sales}, \emph{sale}. \textbf{pongo} — but \emph{pones}, \emph{pone}. \textbf{vengo} — but \emph{vienes}, \emph{viene}.
\end{quote}

So the cost of the whole set is one form each, and it is the form you will use most, because most of what a beginner says is about themselves.

That is a good trade, and it is not an accident of teaching order: the verbs that wore down oddly are the ones people said constantly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
The same two sentences, once about you and once about a friend. Watch which word changes shape and which does not:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Salgo.} — \emph{I'm leaving.} \textbf{Sales.} — \emph{You're leaving.}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Vengo.} — \emph{I'm coming.} \textbf{Viene.} — \emph{He's coming.}
\end{quote}

One word each time, no pronoun, and the only surprise is in the first line of each pair.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Six of the most common verbs in the language, in the person you speak in most. You can now say that you have, do, say, put, leave and come — about yourself, in one word, with no pronoun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item each pair above — first about yourself, then about someone else
  \item all six \emph{yo} forms, then all six \emph{tú} forms, and hear the difference vanish
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which slot in these six verbs is irregular? (\textbf{Only} the \emph{yo} form.) How many words does \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{} take? (\textbf{One} — \emph{salgo}.) Why is that one form worth the trouble? (Because it is the one you will say most.)
\end{tcolorbox}
